title: Vayechi: true kindness (Genesis 47:29)
hookLine: kindness to the dead is called true kindness, since it can't be repaid
last: THE DEATH PORTION IS CALLED LIFE.

cards: A lot of everyday kindness has a little loop in it. I help you move; someday you'll help me. I bring soup when you're sick; you'll remember.
That's not a bad thing. It's how friendships and neighborhoods work. But one kind of help has a loop that can't close.
The person you're helping will never thank you, never return the favor, never even know. Near the end, Jacob asks his son for exactly that kind of help.

teach.h: DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.
teach.b: Jacob knows he's dying. He calls Joseph, asks him to swear an oath, and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt." Take me home.
Bury me with my fathers in the cave they bought, in the land that was promised. In Hebrew, kindly and truly is chesed ve'emet. Kindness and truth.
Kindness done for the dead, he says, is chesed shel emet, true kindness. Why true? Because the one you do it for can never pay you back.
No loop, no thank-you note coming. Kindness with nothing mixed in.
Jewish communities built that idea into an institution: a volunteer group called the chevra kadisha, the holy society.
Its members gently wash the body of someone who has died, dress them in simple white shrouds, and sit with them so they're never left alone before the funeral.

The work happens out of sight, and the one they serve can never thank them. At a traditional burial, mourners and friends take turns shoveling earth into the grave themselves. It's heavy, hard, and nobody can repay it.
And Joseph keeps his oath. When Jacob dies, Joseph and his brothers carry him all the way back to the cave and bury him there.

how: Many Jewish communities have a chevra kadisha, a volunteer burial society that prepares the dead with ritual washing and simple shrouds, and at funerals mourners and friends often help fill the grave themselves.

o: kindness and truth, Jacob's plea to be buried at home
mercy and justice, two sides of how God judges

games.q: inside true kindness — tap the pairs.
p: the holy society that prepares the dead

s: Rashi calls kindness to the dead true kindness
because the one you help can never repay you.
Joseph buried his father in Egypt
he kept his oath and buried Jacob in the family cave in Canaan.
the chevra kadisha is made of paid funeral directors
it's traditionally a volunteer society of community members.

games.q: you're Joseph, ruler of Egypt under Pharaoh. your dying father asks you to carry his body back to Canaan. what do you do?
o: bury him with honors in Egypt, where it's easier.
swear to take him home, and do it.
games.why: Joseph swore, and after Jacob died he and his brothers carried him to the cave of Machpelah and buried him there.

practice: Bring to mind a kind act with no loop to close: tending a grave or a memory, a task for someone who won't know it was you, help for a stranger you'll never see again, picking up what no one will notice was picked up.
Choose one you could actually do, and picture doing it and walking away without a word.

wordCard.voice: Chesed ve'emet. Kindness and truth: Jacob's request to Joseph, which Rashi read as true kindness because it could never be paid back.

orig.note: Hebrew: kindness of truth. Rashi's phrase for kindness to the dead (on Genesis 47:29).

carryVoice: Your line: kindness that can't be repaid. Rashi's word for it is true. That's day two hundred seventeen.
